summarySteps: 1. Implied Volatility Definition ([fact-01]): The volatility parameter equating BSM theoretical price to market price, which would be constant if BSM held perfectly.
2. Put-Call Parity Equality ([fact-02]): European calls and puts sharing identical strike $K$ and maturity $T$ must have the exact same implied volatility.
3. Currency U-Shaped Smiles ([fact-03]): Foreign exchange options display symmetric U-shaped smiles due to leptokurtic exchange rate distributions with fat tails.
4. Equity Volatility Skews ([fact-04]): Stocks and indices exhibit downward-sloping skews where OTM puts trade at substantially higher implied volatilities than OTM calls.
5. Leverage Effect Driver ([fact-05]): Falling stock prices increase financial leverage and equity risk, raising volatility and producing negative skewness.
6. Crashophobia Post-1987 ([fact-06]): Pre-1987 flat smiles were permanently transformed by persistent institutional demand for deep OTM index put crash protection.

7. Breeden-Litzenberger Densities ([fact-07]): Extracts risk-neutral probability density functions directly from call price second derivatives across strikes: $g(K) = e^{rT}  rac{\partial^2 c}{\partial K^2}$.
8. Volatility Surfaces ([fact-09]): Combines strike smiles and term structures into a 3D continuous map $\sigma(K, T)$ for pricing OTC and exotic derivatives.
bottomTakeaway: Real-world markets depart systematically from flat BSM assumptions, forming currency U-shaped smiles and equity skews driven by leverage and Crashophobia, which are modeled via volatility surfaces and advanced stochastic frameworks ([fact-03], [fact-04], [fact-06], [fact-09]).
